doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

chapter: Songwriting and recording Fade to Black
title: Pre-recording whole albums herself before the studio session
summary: She records every idea, plays drums and bass herself, and gives musicians full pre-records and written charts.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Are most of your —these specific songs, I was going to ask about “Eye of the Storm” also. I’m wondering if you mostly record with everybody at the same time?
Wow? You’ve been doing a lot — thank you for these great questions.

Well you know I’ve done a little studio work over the years and when I was watching “Eye of the Storm” and some of your songs have rubato sections, extended sections and then you hit something new, something changes. And I was envisioning the musicians trying to play if you weren’t there. And that would be very difficult it seems.

Well so I have always recorded — I record everything I do. Okay? I record every idea I have. And I have for decades. And I just kind of change with the formatting. So if it was a four-track cassette back in the day or whatever it was, a four-track reel to reel, and then it became an A-dat, then it became this, that and the other. So I’ve always recorded. And in the last I would say the last eight or nine projects of mine I pre-record every idea I have. So I started out using what they call plug-ins or those samples that are part of the

software and fake, you know like they’re loops of instruments but they repeat and repeat and repeat. And they kind of support your idea but they don’t really play your song. So I got away from that. I got away from borrowing, you know bossa nova 101 and all that stuff, and began to play the drums myself and play the bass and play the piano, play the guitar. So I would record that. I would record my drums. Record the bass. Sometimes it would be keyboard bass, sometimes I would actually pick up one of the basses. And sometimes picking up one of the basses informed me, more so than just the keyboard bass. So if I would do this, oh I see, oh I get it, that fingering that’s going to be [inaudible] — so things like that occur and I go back and then I can advance whatever these concepts are that I have in mind. I record everything and I became very fortunate to have met a wonderful recording engineer who embraced my pre-records and embraced what someone might call demos, but they were actually full albums. I would do everything before I would hire the musicians to come in and play. So my musicians, when they come into the studio and we record everything, they’ve already heard my full album where I’ve played everything, which gives them permission and the freedom to now insert their own feeling and ideas because they have an idea already of what I can see. You see? And that’s why we’re rendering these kinds of recordings and these kinds of performances because the musicians are, “Oh Carmen, oh she’s already covered, she’s made this easy for me. I see what she wants there. Oh okay, great.” So that gives them, they can take what I’ve written and because they’re the skilled player on that instrument, I’m not, but they actually stay true, and of course I write everything down note for note. So if the tune needs it I’m going to write out that bass line. Or I’m going to write something on the chart that’s – simile or something. Here’s what I want and then you just be yourself. But these are all the different tools that are now part of my particular approach to getting the music to the stage. Getting the music to the listener. So what we do is we take my pre-records, everybody knows, because I’ve already sent them the printed music, they’ve got my full album and they just kind of go, “Oh you want me to go — oh yeah” and now all these other things occur that I could never have imagined. And that’s what’s beautiful about this process. And that’s what I think — I don’t know if my music really translates that way to my listeners and you kind of have to be in the room when you’re seeing me play it live, but there’s already so much work that has gone into what you hear ultimately and what my engineer — my engineer is so wonderful, he’ll say, “Well Carmen, you know that’s really a nice thing you did there,” you know where I might have had some kind of a plug-in of maybe a brass section or something. And I’ll bring in a tenor player, and I’ll bring in a trumpet player and maybe a trombone for the session, but when we get to the mix he’ll say, “Let’s pull up what you did and let’s see if we can take your plug-ins and somehow I’ll mix it with, you know, with Wallace Roney
